blocks.text: The Physiologus of Epiphanius offers four proofs of the serpent's prudence. First, when it senses old age coming on, it seeks a rock and ῥαγαδαστεύει [ragadasteuei], προκύψας δὲ διὰ τῆς ὀπῆς ὠθεῖται περάσαι, καὶ ἐκβάλλει τὸ γῆρας [prokypsas de dia tēs opēs ōtheitai perasai, kai ekballei to gēras], it slips into a crevice, and, bending forward, strives to pass through the hole, and puts off its old age. And this all assert with one voice. Second, although it flees from a clothed man, when it sees the same man naked, καταθαῤῥεῖ αὐτοῦ [katatharrei autou], it attacks him confidently. This too might seem consistent with reason; yet others expressly teach the opposite. Eustathius in the Hexaemeron: Ἐὰν δὲ γυμνὸν θεάσηται ἄνθρωπον οὐ πρόσεισιν· εἰ δὲ ἐνδεδυμένον, ἐφάλλεται [Ean de gymnon theasētai anthrōpon ou proseisin; ei de endedymenon, ephalletai]; If it has seen a naked man, it does not approach; but if it has seen a clothed one, it attacks. Jerome, or whoever is the author of the Letter to Praesidius under Jerome's name: The snake fears a naked man, and pursues a clothed one. Isidore, book 12, ch. 4: It is said, moreover, that the serpent does not dare to touch a naked man. Damir: ومن عجيب امره انها تهرب من الرجل العريان [wa-min ʿajīb amrihi annahā tahrub min al-rajul al-ʿuryān] Among the marvels of its nature is that it flees from a naked man. And Olaus writes that he has experienced this not rarely. Isidore, he says, offers a favourable word about the nature of serpents, that they never harm a naked and sleeping man [III, 248]: and this happened to me in boyhood and youth, when I very often encountered serpents without harm. The same author offers a third proof of the serpent's prudence: that when attacked by a man it keeps only its head unharmed and exposes the rest of its body. Since I have already said much about this, I shall add only this from Caesarius, Dial. 4, Quaest. 190: Κατευναζόμενος δὲ, καὶ καθεύδων (ὁ ὄφις) τροχίζων ἑαυτὸν, μέσην ὅλου τοῦ σώματος κεφαλὴν ἀσφαλίζεται, οἱονεὶ τειχίῳ τῷ ἐφεπομένῳ ὁλκῷ περιοχυρῶν αὐτήν [Kateunazomenos de, kai katheudōn (ho ophis) trochizōn heauton, mesēn holou tou sōmatos kephalēn asphalizetai, hoionei teichiō tō epheponemō holkō periochyrōn autēn]; When the serpent gives itself to rest in order to sleep, coiling itself up, it secures its head in the middle of its whole body, encircling it with the following length of its body as with a wall. Fourth, when it comes to a spring to drink, οὐ φέρει τὸν ἰὸν, ἀλλά γε ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ νεοττίᾳ, οὕτω καθαρὸς πορεύεται [ou pherei ton ion, alla ge apheis auton en tē neottia, houtō katharos poreuetai], it does not carry its poison along, but leaving it in its nest, it approaches thus pure. The same author sets this out as follows in Haer. 37: Οὐ συμπαραλαμβάνει τὸν ἰὸν μεθ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ, ἀλλὰ ἐν τῷ φωλεῷ καταλιμπάνει, καὶ οὕτως ἐλθὼν λαμβάνει τὸ πόμα τῶν ὑδάτων [Ou symparalambanei ton ion meth' heautou, alla en tō phōleō katalimpanei, kai houtōs elthōn lambanei to poma tōn hydatōn]; It does not bring its poison out with it, but leaves it in its lair, and approaching thus takes its drink of the waters. And Eustathius in the Hexaemeron: Ὅταν δὲ διψήσῃ τὸν ἰὸν πρότερον ἀποτίθεται, καὶ οὕτως ἐκπίνει τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκ τῆς πηγῆς [Hotan de dipsēsē ton ion proteron apotithetai, kai houtōs ekpinei to hydōr ek tēs pēgēs]; When it is thirsty, it first lays down its poison, and so drinks water from the spring: namely, lest the poison, congealed by the water, should kill it, as the author of the Letter to Praesidius adds. Not unlike this is what many write, that the viper, when about to mate with the moray, first vomits out its poison, as if αἰδουμένην τὸν γάμον [aidoumenēn ton gamon], revering the marriage, as Basil says, Hom. 7 on the Hexaem. But Andreas ^{b)} rejects this as fabulous in his book Περὶ τῶν ψευδῶς πεπιστευμένων [Peri tōn pseudōs pepisteumenōn]. Although, besides Basil ^{c)} and Ambrose, it has as authorities Nicander ^{d)}, Aelian ^{e)}, Oppian ^{f)}, Licinius Macer ^{g)}, Achilles Tatius ^{h)}, Philes in the Iambics ^{i)}, and Isidore ^{k)}, and others in no small number.

To these may be added from Pliny that the serpent, when its sight has been dimmed in its winter hiding place, anoints and refreshes its eyes with fennel; and if its scales have grown stiff, it scrapes itself on the thorns of the juniper; and that the dragon relieves its spring nausea with the juice of lettuce. It is more probable that these things happen by natural skill than by some θεηλάτῳ [theēlatō] impulse, as the Arabs imagine. Among them is الزمخشري [al-Zamakhsharī] Azzammachsari, a writer fabulous above others, whose words are: حكي ان الافعي اذا اتت عليها الف سنة عميت وقد الهمها الله ان تمسح عينيها بورق الرازيانج الرطب فير اليها بصرها وربما كان [III, 249] في برية بينها وبين الريف مسيرة ثلثة ايام فتطوي تلك المسافة علي طولها وعلي عماها حتي تهاجم في بعض البساتين علي شجر الرازيانج لاتحظيه فتحك به عينها فترجع باصرة باذن الله تعالي [ḥukiya anna al-afʿā idhā atat ʿalayhā alf sana ʿamiyat wa-qad alhamahā Allāh an tamsaḥ ʿaynayhā bi-waraq al-rāziyānaj al-raṭb fa-yr ilayhā baṣaruhā wa-rubbamā kāna fī barriyya baynahā wa-bayna al-rīf masīrat thalathat ayyām fa-taṭwī tilka al-masāfa ʿalā ṭūlihā wa-ʿalā ʿamāhā ḥattā tuhājim fī baʿḍ al-basātīn ʿalā shajar al-rāziyānaj lā tukhṭīhi fa-taḥukk bihi ʿaynahā fa-tarjiʿ bāṣira bi-idhn Allāh taʿālā] They say that the viper, when it has lived a thousand years, is blinded, and that God inspires it to anoint its eyes with a leaf of fresh fennel, and it recovers its sight. Indeed sometimes it is in the desert, and between it and cultivated land there lies a journey of three days. This distance, however great it is, it traverses, until, having entered some garden, it comes upon a fennel plant, from which it by no means strays, and it rubs its eyes on it, and with God's favour its sight returns to it. Abugiani Thaugidaeus tells a not dissimilar fable: that a kind of serpent is called الشمسية [al-shamsiyya], that is, the Solar, which, when its eyes begin to weaken, turns them toward the sun for the space of an hour on seven successive days, and that by this means its sight is sharpened and strengthened.
